rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Animal adaptations reflect their habitat. Aquatic animals (primary, e.g. fishes; secondary, e.g. whales) have streamlined bodies, gills with countercurrent exchange, lateral lines, and webbed feet. Terrestrial animals show cursorial (running), fossorial (burrowing), or arboreal (tree-dwelling) adaptations, with waterproof skin and lungs.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Aquatic: fusiform body + fins + gills (countercurrent) + lateral line + webbed feet
Terrestrial: waterproof skin + lungs + internal fertilisation + strong limbs
Volant: wings + hollow bones + air sacs + strong pectoral muscles + streamlined body + beak

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Primary aquatic animals were ALWAYS aquatic (fishes); secondary aquatic animals (whales, seals) evolved FROM terrestrial ancestors.  ·  A fusiform (streamlined) body REDUCES water resistance; it is an adaptation for fast swimming.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects a clear aquatic (primary + secondary), terrestrial (cursorial, fossorial, arboreal), and volant adaptation list.  ·  Countercurrent exchange in fish gills is a very common exam point.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Fish (primary aquatic): fusiform body, fins, gills, lateral line, scale-covered skin.  ·  Whale (secondary aquatic): streamlined body, dense bones, blubber, baleen, modified limbs (flippers).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Countercurrent exchange in fish gills allows ~80% O2 uptake efficiency (blood and water flow in opposite directions).  ·  Hollow bones in birds reduce weight for flight; they are still strong (internal struts).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: List aquatic adaptations  ·  Differentiate primary vs secondary aquatic

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Aquatic = A-F-G-L (Adapted, Fusiform, Gills, Lateral line).  ·  Primary = always water; Secondary = land → water (whales).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Explain the aquatic adaptations of a fish.  ·  Differentiate primary from secondary aquatic animals.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: List the terrestrial adaptations (cursorial, fossorial, arboreal).  ·  Explain the volant adaptations of a bird.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Aquatic adaptations (fusiform, gills, lateral line)  ·  Primary vs secondary aquatic  ·  Terrestrial adaptations (cursorial, fossorial, arboreal)  ·  Volant adaptations (wings, hollow bones, air sacs)

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Aquatic: fusiform body, gills (countercurrent), lateral line, webbed feet, fins.  ·  Primary aquatic = always aquatic (fish); secondary = evolved from land (whales, seals).  ·  Terrestrial: cursorial (run), fossorial (dig), arboreal (tree-dwell); waterproof skin, lungs.  ·  Volant: wings, hollow bones, air sacs, strong pectoral muscles, beak.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The fusiform body shape reduces drag by up to ~40% in fast swimmers.  ·  Countercurrent exchange in fish gills allows ~80% O2 extraction; parallel flow would extract only ~50%.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: List the terrestrial adaptations (cursorial, fossorial, arboreal) with examples.  ·  How does countercurrent exchange improve O2 uptake in fish?

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: How does countercurrent exchange work in fish gills?  ·  Give a Nepali example for each adaptation type.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Cheetah (cursorial): long limbs, enlarged nostrils, non-retractable claws for grip, S-spine.  ·  Mole (fossorial): reduced eyes, strong digging forelimbs, cylindrical body, no tail.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The streamlined (fusiform) body of a fish is an adaptation for: → B  ·  Whales and seals are examples of: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Animal adaptation: structural, physiological, and behavioural features that allow an animal to survive in a particular environment.  ·  Aquatic adaptation: primary aquatic (fishes, fully aquatic) and secondary aquatic (whales, seals — originally terrestrial).  ·  Aquatic features: streamlined (fusiform) body, fins, gills (countercurrent exchange), lateral line (fish), webbed feet, dense bones, salt glands.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Countercurrent exchange  ·  Evolutionary adaptation  ·  Nepal examples

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Countercurrent exchange: ~80% O2 uptake in fish gills.  ·  Adaptation is evolutionary (population-level), not individual.  ·  Nepal examples: fish (Terai), snow leopard (cursorial), birds (volant).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Arboreal animals (monkeys) have grasping hands/feet, forward-facing eyes (stereoscopic vision), and a prehensile tail (New World monkeys).  ·  Fossorial animals (moles, earthworms) have reduced eyes, strong forelimbs for digging, and cylindrical bodies.  ·  Orangutan (arboreal): long arms, grasping hands, stereoscopic vision, prehensile tail (New World).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Eagle (volant): feathers, hollow bones, air sacs, strong pectoral muscles, sharp beak and talons.  ·  Hollow bones + air sacs + double respiration are key volant adaptations.  ·  Give a Nepali example for each type (fish, snow leopard, eagle).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Memorise 5 aquatic, 5 terrestrial, and 5 volant adaptations.  ·  Learn countercurrent exchange in fish gills.  ·  List cursorial, fossorial, and arboreal adaptations with examples.
